The Prophet said not to abuse the dead, for they have reached the result of what they sent forward.
When Abu Lahab said to the Prophet, "Perish you all the day," the revelation came: perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he.
Zakat, taken from the rich for the poor, ranks with worship and prayer among deeds leading to Paradise; Abu Bakr vowed to fight anyone withholding it, and Umar agreed.
Unpaid Zakat returns on Judgement Day as trampling animals and a snake; paying it purifies wealth, none is due below set amounts, and Abu Dhar warned hoarders.
Spending wealth rightly is worth envying; Allah grows charity from honest earnings; give now, for before the Hour a time will come when no one accepts charity.
A verse answered those mocking large and small gifts; companions worked as porters to give; half a date shields from Hell, as do daughters treated well; give while healthy.
The wife with the longest hand, first to follow the Prophet, loved charity; alms given unknowingly to a thief, adulteress and rich man may reform them; secret givers are shaded.
A wife giving food from home is rewarded, as are her husband and storekeeper; the best charity is from surplus, dependents first; the giver's hand is better than the beggar's.
The Prophet hurried to give away charity gold before night, had women give jewellery at Eid, urged interceding for those who ask, and told Asma not to withhold money.
Hudhaifa told Umar that failings with family and neighbours are expiated by prayer and charity, and that a closed door, Umar himself, held back tribulation spreading like waves.
Charity and good deeds done before Islam keep their reward; a wife giving food from her husband's house, and an honest storekeeper paying as told, are rewarded alongside the husband.
Angels pray daily for spenders and against misers, whose iron cloak never widens; every Muslim owes charity, by work, help or good deeds; passed-on charity reaches its place.
No Zakat is due below five camels, uqiyas or wasqs; Abu Bakr's letter allows another camel age with adjustment and bars combining or splitting herds; women gave ornaments at Eid.
Abu Bakr's letter set Zakat on camels, sheep and silver, refusing old or defective animals; he would fight over a withheld goat; Mu'adh was to spare people's best property.
Abu Talha gave his beloved Bairuha garden to his relatives on the Prophet's advice; after urging women to give alms, the Prophet told Zainab her husband and children deserved hers.
No Zakat is due on a Muslim's horse or slave.
The Prophet feared the world's splendour for his people: wealth is sweet and green, blessed when given to the poor, orphans and travellers, but taken wrongly it never satisfies.
Zainab earns a double reward for giving Zakat to her husband and the orphans in her care, and Um Salama is rewarded for spending on Abu Salama's children.
Told three men refused Zakat, the Prophet faulted Ibn Jamil, whom Allah made rich, excused Khalid, whose armour was kept for Allah's cause, and said Al-Abbas owes it double.
Whoever refrains from asking, Allah makes content; selling firewood beats begging; wealth taken without greed is blessed; one who keeps begging comes on Judgement Day with a fleshless face.
The truly poor do not beg; Allah hates idle talk, wasted wealth and much asking; the Prophet gave some lest they fall into Hell; cutting firewood beats begging.
On the Tabuk expedition the Prophet estimated a garden's yield at ten wasqs, foretold a strong wind, received gifts from Aila's king, and praised Uhud and the Ansar.
A tenth is due on rain-watered land, a twentieth on well-watered land, none below five wasqs; the Prophet took a charity date from Al-Hasan's or Al-Husain's mouth.
The Prophet forbade selling fruit before it ripens and is safe from blight.
Umar was told not to buy back a horse he gave in charity; the Prophet's family eat no charity, but charity given to Barira became their gift.
Mu'adh was sent to call the People of the Scripture to Allah, prayer and Zakat, sparing their best property and fearing the oppressed's curse; the Prophet blessed those bringing alms.
An Israelite debtor who found no boat sent a thousand dinars to his creditor in a log thrown into the sea, and the creditor found it on sawing the wood.
No compensation is due for one killed by an animal, a well or a mine, but a fifth is due on Rikaz; the Prophet checked his Zakat collector's accounts.
Uraina men given the Zakat camels' milk and urine killed the shepherd and drove off the camels; caught, they had hands and feet cut and eyes branded.
Bringing a newborn for Tahnik, Anas found the Prophet branding the Zakat camels.
Zakat-ul-Fitr: one Sa' of dates, barley, raisins or other food for every Muslim, free, slave, young or old, before the Eid prayer; later people substituted half a Sa' of wheat.
At the Farewell Pilgrimage the Prophet let a Khath'am woman perform the obligatory Hajj for her old father, who could not sit a mount, and turned Al-Fadl's face from her.
The Prophet began saying Labbaik at Dhul-Hulaifa once his mount stood up carrying him.
The Prophet and Anas made Hajj on a packsaddle and Aisha rode one to Umrah; after faith and jihad Hajj Mabrur is best, women's best jihad, wiping away sins.
The Prophet fixed Qarn for the people of Najd, Dhul-Hulaifa for Medina and Al-Juhfa for Sham as the places to assume Ihram.
Yemenis came for Hajj without provisions, saying they relied on Allah, and begged in Medina, so Allah revealed that they should take provision, the best provision being fear of Allah.
The Prophet fixed Dhul-Hulaifa, Al-Juhfa, Qarn and Yalamlam as Miqat for Medina, Sham, Najd, Yemen and passers-by, those within assuming Ihram at home; Umar added Dhatu-Irq.
The Prophet prayed at Dhul-Hulaifa, went by Ash-Shajara and returned by Muarras, and was told Al-Aqiq is a blessed valley for prayer and Ihram of Hajj and Umrah.
Perfume before and during ihram, the Prophet's matted hair, his assuming ihram at the mosque of Dhul-Hulaifa, and the garments a muhrim may not wear.
The Talbiya: its words, begun when the Prophet's mount stood up after praying at Dhul-Hulaifa, said aloud, kept up until stoning Jamrat al-Aqaba, and the Prophet picturing Moses reciting it.
